title: Coffee & Bread
subtitle: Two sample boards: extraction and fermentation

root.title: Coffee Extraction
root.summary: Dissolve the good parts of the bean; leave the rest behind.
root.detail: Only about 1.5% of a cup of coffee is dissolved material — the rest is water. Every brewing technique answers the same question: how do you get more of the tasty part of that 1.5% and less of the harsh part? Four variables constrain each other, and there is exactly one criterion.

nodes.title: Grind Size
nodes.summary: Sets the contact area between water and coffee.
nodes.detail: The finer you grind the same weight of beans, the more surface area you expose, and the faster solubles are carried away. Grind is the most powerful of the four variables — one grind step usually outweighs five degrees of water temperature.

nodes.title: Surface Area
nodes.summary: Halve the particle size and total area doubles.
nodes.detail: Extraction happens at particle surfaces and inner pores. Halving the diameter means eight times as many particles at the same weight and twice the total surface area — extraction speeds up accordingly.

nodes.title: Fines
nodes.summary: Burrs inevitably produce ultra-fine particles.
nodes.detail: Fines extract extremely fast and over-extract quickly, while also clogging the filter bed and slowing the flow. This is the main quality gap between grinders — better burrs give a narrower particle distribution.

nodes.title: Channeling
nodes.summary: Water takes the path of least resistance through the bed.
nodes.detail: Once a channel forms, coffee near it over-extracts while the rest under-extracts — both bad tastes land in the same cup. Uneven distribution, a collapsed bed, or aggressive pouring all trigger it.

nodes.title: Water Temperature
nodes.summary: Sets how fast each compound dissolves.
nodes.detail: Hotter water extracts faster, but not every compound speeds up by the same amount. Temperature is not just a speed dial — it changes the composition of what ends up in the cup.

nodes.title: Dissolution Order
nodes.summary: Acids come out first, sugars next, bitters last.
nodes.detail: Organic acids are small molecules and dissolve first; sugars and Maillard products follow; tannins and some bitter compounds dissolve slowest. Under-extraction tastes sour and over-extraction bitter — it is a matter of order, not concentration.

nodes.title: Follow the Roast
nodes.summary: Hotter water for light roasts, cooler for dark.
nodes.detail: Light roasts are dense and give up solubles reluctantly — they need heat behind them. Dark roasts are porous and release bitter compounds easily; cooler water keeps them in check.

nodes.title: Brew Ratio
nodes.summary: Sets final strength, not extraction itself.
nodes.detail: The ratio of coffee to water controls how concentrated the cup is. At the same extraction yield, a longer ratio simply means a weaker cup. Ratio and yield are two independent axes — conflating them is the classic beginner mistake.

nodes.title: TDS
nodes.summary: Dissolved-solids share; about 1.3 % for pour-over.
nodes.detail: Total Dissolved Solids, measured with a refractometer. It answers "how strong is this cup", not "how much of the bean was extracted" — that second question belongs to extraction yield.

nodes.title: Time & Flow
nodes.summary: Where the other three variables settle their account.
nodes.detail: Contact time is the combined result of grind, pouring technique, and filter — it can rarely be adjusted on its own. When the time looks wrong, the fix is usually a grind change.

nodes.title: The Bloom
nodes.summary: Wet with twice the dose of water; let the CO₂ escape.
nodes.detail: Fresh beans hold a lot of carbon dioxide, which pushes water away and blocks wetting. Pour a small amount first and rest for about 30 seconds so the gas can leave — only then does extraction run evenly.

nodes.title: Early, Mid, Late
nodes.summary: Flavor arrives as acid, then sweet, then bitter.
nodes.detail: Following the dissolution order, the early pour is bright and acidic, the middle carries most of the sweetness and body, and the late phase brings astringency. Where you cut the brew decides where the cup's weight falls.

nodes.title: Extraction Yield
nodes.summary: How much of the bean ends up dissolved in the cup.
nodes.detail: Yield = dissolved solids in the cup ÷ dry dose. It is the only number that lets you compare the outcome of all four variables on one scale, and the starting point for diagnosing any bad cup.

nodes.title: The Golden Cup
nodes.summary: Yield 18 – 22 %, strength 1.15 – 1.45 %.
nodes.detail: A range drawn from large taste panels run by the Specialty Coffee Association in the 1950s. It is not a law of physics — it is where most people's preferences statistically land.

nodes.title: Under vs. Over
nodes.summary: Sharp and salty is under; dry and bitter is over.
nodes.detail: Under-extracted: piercing acidity, short finish, a salty edge. Over-extracted: dry tongue, lingering bitterness, flat flavor. Both in the same cup almost always means channeling.

nodes.title: Refractometer
nodes.summary: Measures TDS; turns taste into a comparable number.
nodes.detail: You can brew well without one, but without one you cannot tell whether today's better cup came from a change in yield or a change in strength.

root.title: Bread Fermentation
root.summary: Let microbes work the dough while the structure holds.
root.detail: Fermentation does two things at once: yeast produces gas that inflates the dough, and the gluten network holds that gas in. The two speeds must match — gas produced too fast bursts the network, and a network too strong refuses to rise. Every recipe and technique tunes this balance.

nodes.title: Yeast
nodes.summary: Turns sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol.
nodes.detail: Yeast metabolizes the fermentable sugars in flour, producing carbon dioxide that inflates the dough plus alcohol and organic acids as flavor precursors. Its activity is acutely temperature-sensitive — roughly doubling with every 10 °C.

nodes.title: Gas Production
nodes.summary: CO₂ dissolves into the dough, then gathers as bubbles.
nodes.detail: The gas first dissolves in the dough's water phase and only comes out of solution at existing gas nuclei once saturated. That is why the number of tiny bubbles worked in during kneading directly decides the crumb of the finished loaf.

nodes.title: Yeast vs. Sourdough
nodes.summary: One is yeast alone; the other adds lactic bacteria.
nodes.detail: Commercial yeast is fast and predictable. A sourdough starter adds lactic acid bacteria that keep producing acid — deeper flavor and longer shelf life, paid for with time and less predictable results.

nodes.title: Sugar Supply
nodes.summary: Flour has little sugar; amylases keep making more.
nodes.detail: Less than 1% of flour is directly fermentable sugar. The rest comes from amylases breaking damaged starch into maltose. That conversion rate decides whether a long fermentation can keep producing gas.

nodes.title: Gluten
nodes.summary: The elastic network that traps the gas.
nodes.detail: Glutenin provides elasticity, gliadin provides extensibility. Under water and mechanical work they cross-link into a mesh; gas gets caught in its cells, so the dough inflates instead of collapsing.

nodes.title: Elastic vs. Extensible
nodes.summary: Two proteins handle opposite jobs.
nodes.detail: Glutenin molecules are large and heavily cross-linked — they snap back. Gliadin molecules are small and mobile — they stretch. Elasticity alone makes dough shrink back; extensibility alone cannot hold the gas.

nodes.title: Stretch & Fold
nodes.summary: Aligns the gluten mid-ferment, without kneading.
nodes.detail: A fold every so often aligns the gluten, evens out temperature, and vents excess carbon dioxide. High-hydration doughs can build strength almost no other way.

nodes.title: Temperature & Time
nodes.summary: Different combinations reach the same proof.
nodes.detail: Temperature and time trade off: cold-and-long reaches the same rise as warm-and-short, but the flavor differs completely — low temperature gives enzymes and lactic bacteria far more working time.

nodes.title: Cold Fermentation
nodes.summary: Cold holds back yeast; enzymes and bacteria go on.
nodes.detail: At 4 °C yeast nearly stops, but amylases and proteases keep working slowly and lactic bacteria keep producing acid. Flavor deepens markedly, and the operating window stretches by hours.

nodes.title: Overproofing
nodes.summary: Acid and enzymes eat the gluten; the gas escapes.
nodes.detail: Overproofed dough shows large surface bubbles, collapses at a touch, and smells distinctly sour. The gluten is already broken — no amount of extra baking saves it. Shorten the time or lower the temperature next round.

nodes.title: Judging Readiness
nodes.summary: Volume, surface bubbles, and the poke test.
nodes.detail: Time is only a reference; the real criterion is the dough's state. Read three signals together: the volume multiple, whether bubbles appear on the surface, and how a poked dimple springs back.

nodes.title: The Poke Test
nodes.summary: Press a dimple; a slow half-rebound means ready.
nodes.detail: Springs back instantly: not ready. Never springs back: gone too far. Rebounding about halfway is the point where gluten tension and internal gas pressure balance.

nodes.title: Volume Ratio
nodes.summary: Use a straight-sided container, not your eye.
nodes.detail: Proof in a transparent straight-sided container and mark the starting height — the multiple reads at a glance. Bowl-shaped containers distort volume judgment badly.

nodes.title: Acidity
nodes.summary: Lactic acid gives depth; acetic acid gives edge.
nodes.detail: Cold and wet doughs lean lactic; warm and stiff doughs lean acetic. For a mellow tang keep it cold and hydrated; for a sharp one, do the opposite.
